Literally, "Ye have become void from Christ," that is, your connection with Christ has become void (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.2">Ga 5:2</reference>). <reference osisRef="Rom.7.2">Ro 7:2</reference>, "Loosed from the law," where the same Greek occurs as here.<div eID="gen35214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whosoever of you are justified--</hi>"are being justified," that is, are endeavoring to be justified.<div eID="gen35215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the law--</hi>Greek, "IN the law," as the element in which justification is to take place.<div eID="gen35216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fallen from grace--</hi>Ye no longer "stand" in grace (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.2">Ro 5:2</reference>). Grace and legal righteousness cannot co-exist (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.4">Ro 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.6">11:6</reference>). Christ, by circumcision (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.21">Lu 2:21</reference>), undertook to obey all the law, and fulfil all righteousness for us: any, therefore, that now seeks to fulfil the law for himself in any degree for justifying righteousness, severs himself from the grace which flows from Christ's fulfilment of it, and becomes "a debtor to do the whole law" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.3">Ga 5:3</reference>). The decree of the Jerusalem council had said nothing so strong as this; it had merely decided that Gentile Christians were not bound to legal observances. But the Galatians, while not pretending to be so bound, imagined there was an efficacy in them to merit a higher degree of perfection (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.3">Ga 3:3</reference>). This accounts for Paul not referring to the decree at all. He took much higher ground. See Paley's Horæ Paulinæ. The natural mind loves outward fetters, and is apt to forge them for itself, to stand in lieu of holiness of heart. <div eID="gen35217" type="x-p"/>

For--</hi>confirming the truth that it is "by faith" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.5">Ga 5:5</reference>).<div eID="gen35221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Jesus Christ--</hi>Greek, "in Christ Jesus." In union with Christ (the Anointed Saviour), that is, Jesus of Nazareth.<div eID="gen35222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor uncircumcision--</hi>This is levelled against those who, being not legalists, or Judaizers, think themselves Christians on this ground alone.<div eID="gen35223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faith which worketh by love--</hi>Greek, "working by love." This corresponds to "a new creature" (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.15">Ga 6:15</reference>), as its definition. Thus in <reference osisRef="Gal.5.5">Ga 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">6</reference>, we have the three, "faith," "hope," and "love." The Greek expresses, "Which effectually worketh"; which exhibits its energy by love (so <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">1Th 2:13</reference>). Love is not joined with faith in justifying, but is the principle of the works which follow after justification by faith. Let not legalists, upholding circumcision, think that the essence of the law is set at naught by the doctrine of justification by faith only. Nay, "all the law is fulfilled in one word--love," which is the principle on which "faith worketh" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.14">Ga 5:14</reference>). Let them, therefore, seek this "faith," which will enable them truly to fulfil the law. Again, let not those who pride themselves on uncircumcision think that, because the law does not justify, they are free to walk after "the flesh" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.13">Ga 5:13</reference>). Let them, then, seek that "love" which is inseparable from true faith (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.8">Jas 2:8</reference>, 12-22). Love is utterly opposed to the enmities which prevailed among the Galatians (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.15">Ga 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.20">20</reference>). The Spirit (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.5">Ga 5:5</reference>) is a Spirit of "faith" and "love" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Ro 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.19">1Co 7:19</reference>). <div eID="gen35224" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17537"/><div sID="gen35238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17537"/>11. Translate, "If I am still preaching (as I did before conversion) circumcision, why am I still persecuted?" The Judaizing troubler of the Galatians had said, "Paul himself preaches circumcision," as is shown by his having circumcised Timothy (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.3">Ac 16:3</reference>; compare also <reference osisRef="Acts.20.6">Ac 20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.24">21:24</reference>). Paul replies by anticipation of their objection, As regards myself, the fact that I am still persecuted by the Jews shows plainly that I do not preach circumcision; for it is just because I preach Christ crucified, and not the Mosaic law, as the sole ground of justification, that they persecute me. If for conciliation he lived as a Jew among the Jews, it was in accordance with his principle enunciated (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.18">1Co 7:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.20">9:20</reference>). Circumcision, or uncircumcision, are things indifferent in themselves: their lawfulness or unlawfulness depends on the animus of him who uses them. The Gentile Galatians' animus in circumcision could only be their supposition that it influenced favorably their standing before God. Paul's living as a Gentile among Gentiles, plainly showed that, if he lived as a Jew among Jews, it was not that he thought it meritorious before God, but as a matter indifferent, wherein he might lawfully conform as a Jew by birth to those with whom he was, in order to put no needless stumbling-block to the Gospel in the way of his countrymen.<div eID="gen35238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>Presuming that I did so, "then," in that case, "the offense of (stumbling-block, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.23">1Co 1:23</reference> occasioned to the Jews by) the cross has become done away." Thus the Jews' accusation against Stephen was not that he preached Christ crucified, but that "he spake blasphemous words against this holy place and the law." They would, in some measure, have borne the former, if he had mixed with it justification in part by circumcision and the law, and if he had, through the medium of Christianity, brought converts to Judaism. But if justification in any degree depended on legal ordinances, Christ's crucifixion in that degree was unnecessary, and could profit nothing (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.2">Ga 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.4">4</reference>). Worldly Wiseman, of the town of Carnal Policy, turns Christian out of the narrow way of the Cross, to the house of Legality. Confirming <reference osisRef="Gal.5.18">Ga 5:18</reference>, by showing the contrariety between the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit.<div eID="gen35258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">manifest--</hi>The hidden fleshly principle betrays itself palpably by its works, so that these are not hard to discover, and leave no doubt that they come not from the Spirit.<div eID="gen35259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which are these--</hi>Greek, "such as," for instance.<div eID="gen35260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Adultery--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen35261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lasciviousness--</hi>rather, "wantonness" petulance, capricious insolence; it may display itself in "lasciviousness," but not necessarily or constantly so (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.21">Mr 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.22">22</reference>, where it is not associated with fleshly lusts) [Trench].
